Now, while Facebook's Libra is a useful way to move money peer to peer, it's actually not really a version of cash, because ultimately the records of transactions and the governance of that network are going to be controlled by the companies that create and oversee it. And that leaves us with the third option, which are so called central bank digital currencies. Now, there's been a lot of efforts underway around the world to build and develop these central bank digital currencies. In China, I think they've been leaders in this regard. We've also seen projects underway in Canada and Europe and in some smaller countries like Venezuela and Iran. There's an interesting design principle that has to go into these kinds of currencies, which is that we need to be able to ensure that governments can oversee large flows of funds to prevent the funding of crime and terrorism and other illicit activities, while also giving individuals at the retail level the ability to make payments peer to peer without necessarily exposing all their information to some central authority. And that's ultimately the biggest challenge. Now what we've suggested is that perhaps the solution is for governments globally to work together to, to create what's called a synthetic global hegemonic currency, which is an awful mouthful and maybe they should consider rebranding. But the idea is fairly simple, which is that individual governments would have their own central bank digital currencies. There would be a global benchmark which would be priced in a basket of those different currencies. And that benchmark would have its own token and you'd be able to use that to spend money peer to peer. And no single government would be able to have perfect information about how individuals are spending that money. So this is one of those things where crises generally tend to accelerate the pace of history. Things that take years or months or years now take days or weeks. To develop and advance. It is a contract that entitles the bearer, the owner of that contract, to a share of a common enterprise and to certain rights, such as the payment of dividends or say, the ability to vote on certain matters like changes of control and so forth. All of those different rules in that contract can be completely digitized and using blockchain. And the reasons to do that are sort of many fold.
